doc.title: Bob Wilber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998

title: The Wildcats as revivalists versus the Condon style
summary: They emulated Oliver, Morton and Armstrong from records, unlike the Chicago players who heard them live.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: There was a comment in one of the jazz books that said that the first American revival group of consequence in the East, talking about The Wildcats.
Did you know you were doing revival at the time?

Well in a sense we did because we were immersed in the music of King Oliver, Jelly Roll Morton, Armstrong Hot Five, and we wanted to play in that style. We didn’t want to imitate their records. We wanted to play in their style but be creative at the same time. And yeah, in a sense it was quite different from the traditional jazz that was happening around New York at that time. I mean that was mostly centered around the Eddie Condon group and Pee Wee Russell and those guys, who were doing their own thing but it was quite different than what we were doing. So it was unique.
Is it possible to put into words what was different about the Condon style and the style that you were emulating?
It’s very hard to describe the difference. The Condon style was a group of musicians who were kids growing up in Chicago in the ‘20s, listening to King Oliver, Armstrong, the

Dodds brothers, and being totally knocked out and inspired by that music. And in their own way playing something which they thought was like it but it turned out different. And what we kids were doing, we were inspired by the records of the same musicians that they had heard in person. We were inspired by the recordings and trying to emulate that sound. So we thought of ourselves as the new Austin High gang.
